tasks.title: Queued heavy runs wait in few calls
tasks.summary: A not-done `bs heavy wait` names its next bound, and the heavy-run fragment's one steer sentence sends every wait on a held lock to the 540 s call, so a queued run costs about 11 turns instead of 43.
tasks.objective: Answer closing-review finding f-bs-optimize/integration-cdcd0b23 (S3, plan v6, against task-14 criterion 3). The heavy-run fragment (.claude/fragments/heavy-run.md, stamped into the eleven carriers by `node scripts/sync-shared-fragments.mjs`) shows the plain `bs heavy wait --file <out>` as the wait. That call returns `"done": false` at its 100000 ms default (heavyWait.ts DEFAULT_WAIT_MS). The fragment offers `--max-wait-ms 540000` beside a Bash `timeout` of 600000 but never steers an agent to it, and the only bound on the number of wait calls is the two-`"holder": null` stop rule. Every wait call is a turn, and `bs heavy run` queues for the lock for up to 1 h (heavyLock.ts DEFAULT_MAX_WAIT_MS 3600000). A run queued behind other holders, plus a suite of about 440 s, can therefore cost up to ceil((3600000 + 440000) / 100000) = 41 wait calls, or 43 turns with the mktemp and the start. That is more than the whole cap of bs-merger (maxTurns 30), which runs the cumulative regression gate, and of bs-verifier and bs-uiux (25), whose templates say `Bash` is there to run the suite. Fix it by steering, without changing the default. (1) heavyWait.ts exports the long bound and its Bash timeout as constants (540000 and 600000), plus the Bash tool's default timeout (120000). Every `"done": false` result carries `"next": {"max_wait_ms": <n>, "bash_timeout_ms": <t>}`. It holds the long pair when the file exists and a holder is named, which means the run is queued or running. It holds the default pair (100000 / 120000) when the holder is null or the file is missing. A done result has no `next`. Exit codes and the fields `done`, `exit`, `tail`, `waited_ms`, `holder`, `idle_ms` and `missing` are unchanged. (2) The fragment keeps `bs heavy wait --file <out>` as its first wait line, so the bare command still fits the Bash tool's default 120 s timeout as written (task-14 pre-code item 1). Its offer sentence ("Pass `bs heavy wait --file <out> --max-wait-ms 540000` only together with a Bash `timeout` of 600000.") is rewritten into one steer sentence, so the long call appears once. The steer says every call is a turn and that `"next"` decides the next call's bound: `next` gives 540000 while a holder is named and the file exists, and that is `bs heavy wait --file <out> --max-wait-ms 540000` with a Bash `timeout` of 600000, never that bound without that timeout. Where `next` and a named holder differ (a missing file), `next` wins and the call stays short. The stop rule (two `"done": false` in a row with `"holder": null`) is unchanged. One queued run then costs at most 1 + ceil((3600000 + 440000 - 100000) / 540000) = 9 wait calls, or 11 turns with the mktemp and the start. (3) heavyLock.ts exports its existing DEFAULT_MAX_WAIT_MS, so the cost test reads the value instead of restating it. The cost test bounds each carrier's heavy runs per dispatch at half its cap. (4) Restamp the eleven carriers with the sync script. No carrier is added or dropped, and no `maxTurns` changes. (5) Update the pins in heavyWait.test.ts and playbookOptimize.test.ts, and the CHANGELOG `## Unreleased` heavy-run entry. Read factory/specs/active/bs-optimize/epic-spec.md first, including the sections "Closing review (plan v5) — changes" (and its subsections "Pre-code review (v6 draft) — changes" and "Verification review (v6 draft) — changes") and "Closing review (plan v6) — changes" (and its subsection "Pre-code review (v7 draft) — changes"). TDD: write the named failing tests first, watch them fail on the unfixed tree, implement minimally, then watch them pass. Every new guard is proven by the mutations its criterion names; the result quotes each mutation's failing output.
acceptance_criteria: Finding f-bs-optimize/integration-cdcd0b23 (the wait names its next bound). Write the failing test first, in factory/orchestrator/test/heavyWait.test.ts. heavyWait.ts exports `LONG_WAIT_MS` = 540000, `LONG_WAIT_BASH_TIMEOUT_MS` = 600000 and `DEFAULT_BASH_TIMEOUT_MS` = 120000. The test asserts that `DEFAULT_WAIT_MS` is still 100000 and that `LONG_WAIT_MS` <= `MAX_WAIT_MS` (still 570000). It asserts that `LONG_WAIT_BASH_TIMEOUT_MS` is at most 600000 and at least `LONG_WAIT_MS` + 30000, and that `DEFAULT_WAIT_MS` + 10000 <= `DEFAULT_BASH_TIMEOUT_MS`. Cases, each with the lock in a temporary lock dir: (a) a not-done result on an existing file whose heavy lock is held by a live pid carries `next: {max_wait_ms: 540000, bash_timeout_ms: 600000}`; (b) so does one whose lock record is corrupt; (c) a not-done result with the holder null carries `next: {max_wait_ms: 100000, bash_timeout_ms: 120000}`; (d) so does one on a missing file while a live holder is named, and that case asserts the holder is non-null, so it cannot pass for want of a holder; (e) a done result has no `next` key. Every other field and every exit code is unchanged: the existing module and verb tests pass unchanged, including the `toEqual` on `{done: true, exit: 75, tail: 'boom'}`. Mutations, each run against the new tests, each failing output quoted in the result: M1a, `next` long with the holder null, fails (c); M1b, `next` long for a missing file, fails (d); M1c, `next` present on a done result, fails (e); M1d, `next` short on a corrupt record, fails (b); M1e, `next` short with a live holder, fails (a).

Finding f-bs-optimize/integration-cdcd0b23 (the verb, and a queued run end to end). Spawned processes run under a temporary `BS_HEAVY_LOCK_DIR` and a temporary HOME. `bs heavy wait --file <out> --max-wait-ms 200` on a file with no `EXIT=` line prints `next` beside `"done": false` and still exits 124. Next, the test pre-holds the heavy lock with a record it writes itself (its own pid, label `someone-else`). It launches the fragment's start command in the background around the suite stand-in. The command is read from .claude/fragments/heavy-run.md with its placeholders filled, not restated. The run stays queued. `bs heavy wait --max-wait-ms 300` exits 124 with `"done": false`, a holder naming `someone-else`, and `next` equal to {max_wait_ms: 540000, bash_timeout_ms: 600000}. When the test removes the record it wrote, the queued run takes the lock (`bs heavy status` names its label). After the release file appears, `bs heavy wait` exits with the child's code and `bs heavy status` prints `{}`. Every child is killed or awaited in `afterEach`. No test signals a pid it did not start or removes a lock record it did not write. Mutation M2: under M1e (`next` short with a live holder), the queued-run case fails; its output is quoted in the result.

Finding f-bs-optimize/integration-cdcd0b23 (the fragment steers, and stays small). Write the failing pins first, in factory/orchestrator/test/playbookOptimize.test.ts. (a) .claude/fragments/heavy-run.md keeps `bs heavy wait --file <out>` as the first line that starts `bs heavy wait`. That is the plain call, which fits the Bash tool's default timeout as written (task-14 pre-code item 1). (b) The offer sentence "Pass `bs heavy wait --file <out> --max-wait-ms 540000` only together with a Bash `timeout` of 600000." is gone, rewritten into one steer sentence. A pin asserts that the fragment shows exactly one `bs heavy wait` call carrying `--max-wait-ms`, and that it sits in the steer sentence. (c) The steer sentence says every wait call is a turn and that `"next"` decides the next call's bound. It names a held lock (`"holder"`) as the case where `next` gives 540000, and that call is `bs heavy wait --file <out> --max-wait-ms 540000` with a Bash `timeout` of 600000, never that bound without that timeout. The sentence never states the long call as following from a named holder alone, so where the two differ (a missing file with a live holder), `next` wins and the call stays short. The new pin requires, in that one sentence, `"next"` as the deciding signal, the holder condition, the long call, the 600000 timeout and the turn reason; it replaces the test 'pairs a longer --max-wait-ms with a Bash timeout of 600000' and is no weaker. A second pin, the order pin, makes the long call governed by `"next"`: in the steer sentence the first `"next"` comes before the long call, and no `"holder"` comes before the long call. The holder condition can therefore appear only after the long call, as the case where `next` gives 540000 (for example: "... call again with the bound its `"next"` gives: for 540000 that is <long call> with a Bash `timeout` of 600000, never that bound without that timeout, which `"next"` gives only while the file exists and a `"holder"` is named"). The steer does not copy the holder-alone clause of the cdcd0b23 line in the epic spec ("once a `"done": false` names a `"holder"`, each next call is <long call>"). That clause is superseded, and with `"next"` added to its sentence it still fails the order pin. (d) Size, measured on the whitespace-flattened fragment split after each '. ', with words counted as space-separated tokens. The steer sentence (the one sentence holding `--max-wait-ms`) has at most 60 words. The rest of the fragment has at most 297 words: v6's fragment at e4341588 had 313 words, 16 of them in the offer sentence. The test holds 297 as a named constant with that derivation in a comment, so a later edit that grows the fragment must raise it on purpose. (e) The stop rule keeps its wording, and every other fragment pin passes unchanged. heavyWait.test.ts's three tests under 'each bs heavy wait call the fragment shows fits its Bash tool timeout' pass unchanged on the new fragment. A new assertion there reads the steer's bound and timeout and asserts they equal `LONG_WAIT_MS` and `LONG_WAIT_BASH_TIMEOUT_MS`. Mutations, each failing by name with its output quoted in the result: M3a, the steer without the holder condition; M3b, the steer without the 600000 timeout (the heavyWait.test.ts sentence check fails too); M3c, the old offer sentence kept beside the steer, so the long call appears twice; M3d, a steer sentence of 61 words; M3e, one word added to any other sentence; M3f, a steer bound of 500000 that differs from `LONG_WAIT_MS`; M3g, a steer that does not name `"next"` as what decides the bound, failing the names-next pin; M3h, the cdcd0b23 line's holder-alone clause with `"next"` added to the same sentence (`"holder"` before the long call), which passes the names-next pin and fails the order pin by name, so M3g and M3h give different failing outputs.

Finding f-bs-optimize/integration-cdcd0b23 (a dispatch's heavy-run turns fit each carrier's cap). Write the failing test first, in heavyWait.test.ts. Cost of one run: from the steer's bound (read from the fragment), the module's `DEFAULT_WAIT_MS`, heavyLock.ts's now-exported `DEFAULT_MAX_WAIT_MS` (3600000; its value and every use unchanged) and a 440000 ms suite (a named constant: the epic's measured full suite), the test computes the worst-case turns one heavy run costs a carrier that follows the fragment: 1 (mktemp) + 1 (start) + 1 (the plain wait) + ceil((DEFAULT_MAX_WAIT_MS + 440000 - DEFAULT_WAIT_MS) / steered bound). That is 11 today. Runs per dispatch: the test holds `HEAVY_RUNS_PER_DISPATCH`, the heavy runs each carrier's template or brief directs in one dispatch, as the epic spec "Closing review (plan v6) — changes", subsection "Pre-code review (v7 draft) — changes", item 1, states them: coder 3 (a full-suite gate run and two re-runs after fixes), tester 2 (`test_unit` and `test_e2e`), merger 1 (the cumulative regression gate; bs-merger.md:52-58 returns after it, and a re-run after the queue moved is the merge queue's own, under `bs queue run`, never the merger's), wave-runner 1, and auditor, grader, reviewer, security-reviewer, spec-reviewer, uiux and verifier 1 each (a probe: their templates say `Bash` is there to run the suite). Its keys must equal the carriers derived from the templates with templateFragments.ts's `parseSharedRegions`, not a hand list. A carrier missing from the table, or a table entry that is no carrier, fails by name. Bound: for every carrier, runs x per-run cost <= floor(maxTurns / 2), with `maxTurns` read through agentsSync.ts's `readTemplateMaxTurns`. That leaves at least half of each cap for the role's own work and its result. Today's numbers: bs-merger 11 <= 15, which leaves 19 turns for its ~10 conflict turns, the result write and the return (10 + 11 + 2 = 23 <= 30); bs-tester 22 <= 30; bs-verifier and bs-uiux 11 <= 12; bs-coder 33 <= 75. A failure names the role, its runs, the per-run cost and the limit. Mutations, each failing output quoted in the result. M4a: the unfixed fragment fails with 'no steer sentence', because no sentence pairs a holder with a `--max-wait-ms` call. M4b: a steer bound of 100000 fails naming, among others, bs-uiux and bs-verifier with 43 turns against a limit of 12. M4c: one carrier (bs-verifier) dropped from the derived list fails the table cross-check by name. M4d: bs-tester's runs raised to 3 fails naming bs-tester with 33 against 30. The null (M4a) and the weak steer (M4b) give different outputs.

Finding f-bs-optimize/integration-cdcd0b23 (nothing the hooks deny). The test reads the steered call from the fragment's steer sentence and fills `<out>` the way the existing hook test does. Sent in the foreground with Bash `timeout: 600000`, the call gets no deny from `dietDecision`. `decideHookPayload` allows it for an unleased session and under each of the six judge leases. The existing hook tests are extended, and their three existing commands stay allowed. guardrails.yml and policy.ts are not edited. Mutation M5: with `; sleep 5` appended to the steered call the test reads, the `dietDecision` assertion fails; its output is quoted in the result.

Finding f-bs-optimize/integration-cdcd0b23 (stamps, carriers, caps, changelog). `node scripts/sync-shared-fragments.mjs` restamps exactly the eleven carriers, and `--check` then reports 0 drifted. The carrier set is unchanged: every Bash-holding judge template says `Bash` is there to run the suite (bs-verifier.md:22, bs-uiux.md:28), so each may start a heavy run and keeps the rule (epic D9). templateFragments.test.ts passes unchanged, as do the eleven-carrier, Bash-holder and no-restatement tests in playbookOptimize.test.ts. No template's `maxTurns` line changes. The CHANGELOG `## Unreleased` heavy-run entry says two things: a not-done wait carries `"next"`, and while a holder is named the agent waits with `--max-wait-ms 540000` under a Bash `timeout` of 600000. docCommands and the CHANGELOG tests pass.

Gate, run from the worktree root on the task's own tree, each output read to its end: `pnpm run test` (the full root suite, never a scoped vitest run), `pnpm run typecheck`, `pnpm run typecheck:test`, `pnpm biome check .`, `node scripts/sync-shared-fragments.mjs --check`. The role templates the harness loads come from the main clone and predate the heavy-run rule, so the full suite runs as the wave brief directs. It runs as a background task under the heavy lock, writing a fresh output file outside the worktree whose last line is `EXIT=<n>` on a line of its own. It is waited for in foreground calls that each end inside the Bash tool's timeout and use no `sleep`. The result quotes that file's final summary lines and its `EXIT=0`. All five green before hand-back. Mutation runs are scoped vitest runs of the touched test files, which are not full-suite runs and take no lock, and every mutation is reverted before the gate runs.

functional_clauses: `bs heavy wait` keeps its default bound of 100000 ms, its 570000 ms ceiling, its `--max-wait-ms` validation and every exit code. A done result exits `<n>` from the file's final `EXIT=<n>` line (75 stays `heavy.wait-timeout`), and a not-done result exits 124. `done` says whether to call again; the exit code does not. `next` says only which bound the next call uses.

`next` appears on every `"done": false` result and on no other: `{"max_wait_ms": 540000, "bash_timeout_ms": 600000}` when the file exists and a holder is named (a live lock record, or a corrupt one), `{"max_wait_ms": 100000, "bash_timeout_ms": 120000}` when the holder is null or the file is missing. Its values come from heavyWait.ts's exported constants. It is computed from the holder read and the file probe the not-done path already does, with no new read.

heavyWait.ts keeps every existing export by name and meaning (cli.ts imports `DEFAULT_WAIT_MS`, `MAX_WAIT_MS` and `heavyWait`). The only declaration that changes is `HeavyWaitResult`'s not-done variant, which gains `next`.
`bs heavy wait` stays read-only. It takes no lock, writes nothing, spawns nothing and runs no shell, polls at most every 2000 ms, and reads only the file's end.

The fragment's plain `bs heavy wait --file <out>` stays its first wait line. The offer sentence is rewritten into the steer, so the long call appears once, in the steer sentence, beside the Bash `timeout` of 600000. The steer makes `next` the deciding signal; where a named holder and `next` differ, `next` wins. The stop rule, exit 75 / holder / no blind retry, the three self-locking verbs and the scoped-run exemption are kept word for word.
`bs heavy run`, the lock's behaviour and its 1 h default wait are unchanged. The only change to heavyLock.ts is the `export` keyword on the existing DEFAULT_MAX_WAIT_MS.

The fragment stays the rule's one home (epic D9): brief compose, wave.md and dispatch.md gain no copy. Agent templates change only inside their `heavy-run` SHARED region, written by `node scripts/sync-shared-fragments.mjs`, never by hand. No carrier is added or dropped, and no template's `maxTurns` changes.
cli.ts and usage.ts are not edited: the verb prints the module's result as it is, and its usage line stays true.
Nothing the diet hook denies is introduced (no foreground `sleep` of 2 s or more). guardrails.yml and policy.ts are not edited, and the sandbox is never widened.
Out of scope and recorded as an accepted gap (epic spec, pre-code review (v7 draft), item 4): an agent whose own start died while another holder keeps the lock. The stop rule does not change for it.
nonfunctional_clauses: Quality first, speed second, tokens third (epic decision 6): nothing in this task removes, skips or makes conditional a judge, round, verifier pass or gate check, and no role's model is downgraded.
Open source: no other project's name in code, tests, fixtures or docs; use `project-a` / `<project>`.
Stay inside this task's claims; every other file is read-only, including factory/specs/** (the epic spec is the planner's).
Tests that spawn processes clean up every child they start (killed or awaited in an `afterEach`/`finally`) and never signal a pid they did not start.
Tests that take a lock point it at a temporary directory (`BS_HEAVY_LOCK_DIR` or the `lockDir` option), never the machine's real locks under `~/.blacksmith/locks`.

The fragment is stamped into eleven system prompts. The steer sentence has at most 60 words, and the rest of the fragment at most 297 (v6's 313 less the 16-word offer sentence it replaces). Both are pinned by criterion 3 (d).

Verify every new guard by mutation before trusting its pass: M1a-M1e, M2, M3a-M3h, M4a-M4d and M5, as the criteria name them. Each must fail by name, and the result quotes each failing line. A mutation is reverted before the next one and before the gate.
